articles.title: Man who used fraudulent passport to get in and out of Canada 16 times handed 2-year sentence
articles.summary: A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.

image.caption: Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act by using a fraudulently issued passport to enter and exit the country 16 times. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Ghanaian man who used a fraudulent Canadian passport to leave and re-enter the country 16 times has been sentenced to two years in prison for citizenship fraud.
Jefferson Zormelo pleaded guilty to violating Canadian Citizenship Act
Jefferson Zormelo, 22, pleaded guilty earlier this year to violating the Canadian Citizenship Act.
On Monday in Calgary, Justice Karen Molle said Zormelo’s act “attacks the integrity of the Canadian citizenship regime.”
“The offence jeopardized public safety and our national security,” noted Molle. “Fraudulent use of Canadian passports affects Canada’s international reputation.”
With credit for the time he’s served since his arrest, Zormelo has about 14 months left behind bars.
Used airports in Montreal, Toronto, Halifax
Zormelo came to Canada on a study permit in 2021.

In 2024, when authorities determined he was no longer enrolled in school, an exclusion order was issued for his removal from the country, according to an agreed statement of facts filed as part of the guilty plea.

He then obtained identification documents, including a proof of citizenship under a false name, and used that to get a Canadian passport, which was issued under the name Mitchell Leblanc in December 2024.
Over the next 15 months, Zormelo then entered and exited Canada through Montreal's, Toronto's and Halifax’s international airports using the Leblanc passport a total of 16 times.
In April 2026, he was arrested by Canada Border Services Agency officers in Calgary after presenting a fake permanent residency card in the Leblanc name to officials at the U.S. Consulate.
Officers then searched Zormelo's hotel room and discovered, among other things, the fraudulent passport.
'Clever criminals pose a greater risk'
Prosecutor Tyler Lord had sought a five-year prison sentence.
Defence lawyer Devin Frank asked the court to consider a time-served sentence of nine months in jail, arguing his client experienced a difficult upbringing in Ghana, which involved poverty and abuse.
The judge noted Zormelo was "desperate to live and work in Canada."

items: Government abruptly suspends citizenship certificates issued under 'lost Canadians' law

blocks.text: In the end, Molle outlined a number of aggravating factors, including the fact that Zormelo used his intellect to commit the “sophisticated, elaborate” fraud.
“Clever criminals pose a greater risk to public safety,” said Molle.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - media reports
articles.summary: The ruling means prosecutors can pursue the case, meaning they could reduce charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.

blocks.text: A Massachusetts judge has denied motions to dismiss the murder case of Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, according to local US media.
The judge's ruling comes after Clancy's defence team requested dismissal of the case after her first trial ended in a mistrial in September, when a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
Clancy's defence team had filed three motions, including one to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.

Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the August murder trial, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to double jeopardy, according to Reuters news agency.
Sullivan also denied a motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
The judge scheduled a hearing for 16 November to discuss when to hold a second trial. He has previously suggested it could begin in March.

articles.title: Hegseth to hold press briefing after U.S. House Republican moves to impeach him
articles.summary: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump…

image.caption: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth in Cebu, the Philippines, on Oct. 28. Fellow Republican Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote in the U.S. House on impeaching Hegseth. (Jam Sta Rosa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
Secretary of War expected to hold news conference Tuesday morning

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.

The impeachment resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, the deadly strikes on boats allegedly transporting drugs in waters near South America, and attempts to prosecute two Congress members who served in the military and recorded a video advising service members they were not obliged to follow illegal orders.

Massie, who was defeated by a Trump-backed challenger in a primary earlier this year, said the secretary's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanours" and his leadership at the Pentagon "thus warrants impeachment."
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference from the Pentagon on Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — on the impeachment threat.
GOP congressman urges vote on impeachment of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth
Vote would be 'terrible look': departing Speaker
Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent this outcome, and warned lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth while the U.S. is engaged in military actions in the Middle East.

"Impeaching a cabinet secretary right now, especially the Department of War in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that," said Johnson, who will give way to a new Democratic House Speaker in January.
"We don't impeach cabinet secretaries for political gain or for cheap tricks, and I think that's what this is and I think everybody knows it."
Hegseth defends actions
Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Massie said Hegseth has violated international norms and the U.S.'s own conventions of war in Iran.
"It's to the disadvantage and the dishonour of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflict," he said.

items: Hegseth defends record as Pentagon chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment

blocks.text: Hegseth said earlier Monday he's eager to litigate the military actions that he and U.S. President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders.

"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic," Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis' attacks on shipping in the Middle East.
Hegseth gave a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30, but has not held a media availablity since May. (Alex Wong/The Associated Press)

The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress. Massie pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the conflict.

"The reality is, we're not indicting him for being bad at his job," said Massie outside the Capitol later in the day. "In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings."
Hegseth waves off impeachment push as 'noise'
Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the possible impeachment push.

"There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long."
"My team, we're not worried about the noise — it's what I told the troops, too — don't worry about the noise," he said.
On Monday, Trump called Massie a "stone-cold loser" and said he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached.

In an interview with C-SPAN, he said if any Republicans voted for impeachment, he'd be "disappointed in them," while arguing that "Pete has won two wars," referring to the lightning strike operation in Venezuela and the military campaign against Iran.
Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats prepare for political war
Hegseth insists 'Iran is devastated'
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."

Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

items: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report
UN mission finds 'grounds to believe' U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre

blocks.text: Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks.

With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and insisted that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."

Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: The family business: Arnold Schwarzenegger’s son muscles into top 5 at bodybuilding competition
articles.summary: More than 60 years after Arnold Schwarzenegger first flexed his stuff on a bodybuilding stage, his youngest son is continuing the dynasty of muscle, scoring in the top five during his professional…

image.caption: Joseph Baena, the 29-year-old son of Arnold Schwarzenegger, has made his professional debut as a bodybuilder, decades after his father made a career out of muscle. (Joseph Baena/Instagram and Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

More than 60 years after Arnold Schwarzenegger first flexed his stuff on a bodybuilding stage, his youngest son is continuing the dynasty of muscle, scoring in the top five during his professional debut over the weekend.
Joseph Baena, 29, follows his father's muscular example
Joseph Baena competed in the classic physique category at the INBA PNBA Pro/AM World Cup in California on Saturday.
The 29-year-old placed fifth and said in a video on Instagram that he was happy to have achieved his goal of cracking the top five.
"I'm extremely proud of myself," said Baena, who only started competing this year. "It was an incredible experience for my first show as a pro."
This was the third-ever show for Baena, son of bodybuilder-turned-actor-turned-politician Schwarzenegger and Mildred Baena.
Under a video Baena shared on Instagram of his posing routine at the competition, several commenters noted, "Like father, like son."

It’s perhaps no surprise that the son of a man who became famous for being impressively jacked is following in his footsteps. Schwarzenegger’s physique scored him the title of Mr. Universe five times at professional bodybuilding competitions in the 60s and 70s, and he remains one of the most enduring names associated with bodybuilding.

items: Record-smashing powerlifter, 68, says she lives for the 'clang' of the weights

blocks.text: His 1977 docudrama, Pumping Iron, is credited with giving bodybuilding more exposure and having it treated more widely as a sport. High-profile roles for Schwarzenegger in Hollywood action films like Conan the Barbarian (1982) and The Terminator franchise further pushed muscle into the mainstream.

Arnold Schwarzenegger poses alongside dancers from the famous Parisian cabaret Le Paradis Latin on May 20, 1977, during the Cannes Film Festival in southern France. Schwarzenegger was there to present the docudrama Pumping Iron. (Raph Gatti/ AFP via Getty Images)

In his video reflecting on the competition, Baena said that bodybuilding was a solo sport where "it all comes down to your own discipline," but noted that he had a lot of support from family and friends.
"My father always says there's no such thing as a 'self-made man.' I have people in my corner," he said.
Baena called Schwarzenegger "the best training partner," in an interview with GQ earlier this year, saying his father makes sure he doesn’t "slack off in the gym."
He added that his father gave him "the bodybuilding encyclopedia" when he was in college, and that it sparked his interest in the sport.
Schwarzenegger and Baena attend Netflix's Los Angeles premiere of Fubar Season 2 on June 11, 2025. (Charley Gallay/Getty Images for Netfix)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Skydance replaces James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios chiefs following Warner Bros. takeover
articles.summary: In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.

image.caption: The two DC Studios chiefs are being replaced following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros., after four years at the helm of the superhero franchise (FILE: 13/10/2026)Image: Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios after four years, Skydance Motion Picture Group announced on Monday.
Their departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros, just a year after Gunn's "Superman" reached cinemas.
Who will replace Gunn and Safran?

Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison has chosen Jeremy Latchman, a former Marvel Studios executive, to lead DC Studios. He is set to become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1.
Latchman will oversee the next phase of DC's film and television business, which includes characters such as Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman.
He was involved in major Marvel productions including "Iron Man" and "The Avengers," and previously worked with Gunn and Safran on Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" movie.
What did Gunn and Safran achieve?
Gunn and Safran took charge of DC Studios in 2022, tasked with rebuilding the franchise and creating a more unified cinematic universe.
Their first film, "Superman," earned nearly $619 million (€553 million) worldwide in 2025.

But their second release, "Supergirl," flopped in June 2026, taking around $126 million worldwide against a reported production budget of $170 million. The horror-inspired "Clayface" followed in October.
Overall, DC has struggled to match immense profits and cultural impact made by Marvel in the early years of its own cinematic universe.

blocks.caption: 'Superman' was the first major theatrical release under DC Studios chiefs James Gunn and Peter SafranImage: DC Studios/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of," Ellison said in a statement.
"We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."
Gunn is currently completing "Man of Tomorrow," a sequel to "Superman." Other DC projects in development include "The Batman: Part II" and the television series "The People v. Gorilla Grodd."
Although Gunn and Safran will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans, several projects developed under their leadership remain in production.
Was Gunn's Superman too 'woke' for conservatives?
Gunn's "Superman" sparked a political controversy in 2025 after the director described the superhero as an immigrant and emphasized themes of human kindness.
Conservative commentators accused the film of being "woke."
Skydance CEO Ellison has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump. Ellison has acknowledged having a good relationship with the administration but denied politicizing the company.
There is no evidence that the controversy surrounding "Superman" played a role in Gunn and Safran's replacement.

articles.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth faces impeachment push over Iran war
articles.summary: Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

image.caption: Hegseth previously told reporters he was not worried about the 'noise,' referring to rumors of his impeachmentImage: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as pressure builds on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

The resolution proposed by the Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of conducting the war illegally without congressional authorization. Massie also claims Hegseth has abused his powers as the head of the Pentagon.
Massie is using a special procedure that could see the US House of Representatives vote on the resolution within two days, with the legislative chamber still dominated by Republicans.
Trump told reporters at the White House that Hegseth had done a "good job" and had "won" wars in Venezuela and Iran.
"I'll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge," Trump said.
How has Hegseth responded?
Earlier on Monday, Hegseth sought to downplay rumors about the push against him.
"My team, we’re not worried about the noise," he told reporters.
Hegseth said he would hold a press conference Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — and defended the war as necessary, even if unpopular.
Who supports impeachment?
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries backed the effort Sunday.
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," he told ABC News. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."
Some Republicans have signaled they might support the charges. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding.
The push follows Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices. Republicans retain control until January 3.
Would impeachment remove Hegseth from office?
Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House and amounts to bringing formal charges. Removal would require a Senate trial and conviction by two-thirds of senators present.
Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold.
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?

articles.title: Millions fill Buenos Aires streets to welcome Pope Leo XIV
articles.summary: The Pope celebrated an outdoor Mass in Argentina's capital, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, just three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV celebrated an outdoor Mass in Buenos Aires, Argentina, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
An estimated 2.5 million people filled the streets to welcome him and attend the historic Mass.

articles.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
articles.summary: An estimated 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care…

image.caption: Argentina had not hosted a papal visit since 1987, despite being the homeland of Leo's predecessor, FrancisImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.
"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.
What did Pope Leo say about Milei's spending cuts?
Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.
He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.
"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

blocks.caption: Some worshippers had camped overnight to secure a place at Argentina's first papal massImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.
Argentina declares national holiday over Pope Leo's visit
Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.
Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.
Pope's message for Milei
In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.
Where is the pope traveling next?
The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis, despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.
Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.
The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."
The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
articles.summary:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families

Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke

blocks.text: Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”
Among the casualties was an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”
Video posted to social media showed residents using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, searching for people trapped underneath using flashlights.

blocks.caption: Palestinians remove sand at the site of the deadly sand bank collapse. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for the displaced.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.
Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

blocks.caption: Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks following the collapse of a large sandstone slab. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.
Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said over 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothinghad reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.

articles.title: Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction
articles.summary: The outlet has been evicted from its offices of three decades and says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

blocks.text: Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities.
For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country.
On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process".
The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure.

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.

blocks.text: At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up.

blocks.text: France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
Speaking at a news conference, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.

He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.

Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

articles.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
articles.summary: Trump made the claims, without evidence, on Truth Social on Monday.

blocks.text: In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.
He has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers even as counting continues in some races.

articles.title: French officials blame Iran for supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: The recent cyberattack on supermarkets in France was organized by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has said, describing the hacking as "unprecedented."

image.caption: Stores in several countries across Europe recently experienced fridge and freezer issuesImage: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO

blocks.text: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attacks on French supermarkets last month came from Iran, and were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a powerful paramilitary force loyal to the Iranian regime.
"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," Barrot said, adding "we will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The comparatively simple cyberattack nevertheless had dramatic consequences, spoiling large quantities of produce and in some cases setting temperatures so high that refrigeration units caught fire.
It was launched on October 11 but last week a series of similar incidents affected French supermarkets and authorities even reported a failed attempt to hack cooling units at blood banks.
This is a breaking news story. More to follow...

articles.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
articles.summary: The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.

image.caption: Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia.

The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.

Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Founding editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work with the paperImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech
2021 Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.

"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."

Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.
What is Novaya Gazeta?

Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.

The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.

They included Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.

Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.

blocks.caption: The paper moved online soon after Russia's invasion of UkraineImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.
Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?

Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.
"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."
"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.
Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia, as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.
One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."
Russia's shadow war: How Europe fights back

articles.title: Ice hockey: Norway says it's been kicked out of World Juniors in favor of Russia
articles.summary: The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament – to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a…

image.caption: The last time Germany hosted the World Championship in 2017, Russia won the bronze medalImage: Andreas Dick/Beautiful Sports/IMAGO

blocks.text: With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th (of 10) participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) said that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had informed it that it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to last month's Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta beginning on December 26. Still, Swiss Ice Hockey responded to Norway's statement, saying it's team would not face Russia at the World Juniors – as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.
However, it is far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Mark Carney said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the NIHF hope that its team could still play in the upcoming World Juniors. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.
"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten said.
"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."
Hosts Germany continue to explore options

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed – or not – with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship next May.

"We intend to host the World Championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.
While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.
Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility – if only as a last resort.
On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.
Could Munich's Olympic bid be a factor?
It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee – opening the door for their return to competition, despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games – like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) – to follow its lead.
Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

articles.title: Russia's top independent newspaper closes under relentless government pressure
articles.summary: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials.

image.caption: Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta, holds a poster in support of jailed reporters outside the outlet's office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a relentless campaign by the authorities, in Moscow on Monday. (Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters)

blocks.text: World
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials.
Novaya Gazeta, last major independent media critical of Kremlin, saw staff killed, attacked in Putin's Russia

It was the last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin that remained active in Russia. Others closed or moved their operations abroad after President Vladimir Putin launched Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In a statement published Oct. 30, the newspaper said the Russian authorities and the security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations."

"Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime," the newspaper said. "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot."
The newspaper was launched in 1993 by Dmitry Muratov and the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, using money from Gorbachev's 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.
6 journalists killed

Novaya Gazeta quickly became known for its fierce reporting and dedication to uncovering Russian human rights abuses and corruption. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin's first term as president. She was fatally shot in her apartment building in 2006.
On the newspaper's final day in its office Monday, journalists slowly removed the portraits of their slain colleagues from the newsroom where reporters and editors planned their work.

Sergei Sokolov, editor-in-chief of the Novaya Gazeta daily, collects portraits of slain journalists from the offices as the newspaper closes down in Moscow on Monday. (Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images)
Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the outlet's closure almost every day for the past 4½ years.
"It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office — this is our home, and we're losing it," she said.
Novaya Gazeta had faced growing government pressure as the Kremlin cracked down on critics, with repression sharply intensifying after the start of the conflict in Ukraine.
Editor attacked on train

Longtime editor-in-chief Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, was attacked on a train in 2022 by an assailant who poured red paint over him, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being named a "foreign agent" by Russian authorities. The designation carries strong pejorative connotations in the country and can bring additional government scrutiny.

The newspaper was fined after it was accused of discrediting Russia's armed forces, and it also was declared a foreign agent. Authorities blocked all of its online platforms, seized its printing house, revoked its media registration and shut down the donation system that allowed it to receive support from readers.
Kremlin tightens grip on Russians' access to media with misinformation law
In a final blow, the newspaper was ordered to clear out its Moscow offices.
As reporters left the building and gathered in the street, a new sign was affixed atop the nameplate that once announced the newspaper's office. It read, "Here lived Novaya Gazeta."
Sergei Sokolov, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief, said he believed the newspaper would return one day "with renewed strength."

"We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues."
'You cannot blame citizens for this'
Muratov said people needed to understand ​that it was the Kremlin that was to blame for waging the war and suppressing free speech.

"We cannot blame the citizens themselves for this — especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation. I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he said.

items: Canada's Russian envoy returns with advice on how to hit back against Putin
Russia denies think-tank assessment that 1.2 million of its troops have been killed or injured in Ukraine war

blocks.text: The Kremlin defends the need for censorship laws, denies there are any ​political prisoners and says that Russia is taking necessary action at a time of war to prosecute people engaged in subversive activity.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the newspaper's closure was part of a "rotational process" ⁠in a fiercely competitive media environment.
Some of Novaya Gazeta's staff left Russia in 2022 and opened a separate project, Novaya Gazeta Europe. The new outlet has been sharply critical of the Kremlin and its military action in Ukraine.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?
articles.summary: Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

image.caption: The Berlin Wall came down on November 9, 1989Image: Norbert Michalke/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the wall. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.
Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.
Winter shoes? Candy!
Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.
In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.
The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalls. "I think it was just too fast for people."

blocks.caption: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, author Lea Streisand was finally able to visit her great-grandmother in the western part of BerlinImage: Marlene Gawrisch

blocks.text: The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Vorpommern, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany’s most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.
"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in her: "I quickly realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalls. "That made me afraid."

blocks.caption: Photo artist Simon Menner is interested in how images are instrumentalized in advertising, propaganda and warfareImage: Simon Menner

blocks.text: Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As he put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.
In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."
The Stasi's photo treasure trove

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns him — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.
His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Sometimes eerie, sometimes curious, even absurd.

blocks.caption: Before searching an apartment, the Stasi would take Polaroid photographs so that they could subsequently restore the rooms to the state in which they had found themImage: Simon Menner/BStU 2013

blocks.text: Simon Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success."
In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany’s past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

According to Lea Streisand, literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she says. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Anke Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

blocks.caption: 'May Day' from the comic book 'Comrade Cuckoo' by Anke FeuchtenbergerImage: Anke Feuchtenberger

blocks.text: The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.
The artist says she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the Wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty. Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, says Feuchtenberger.
What does the future hold?

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than the West German man. "In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," says Simon Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he said, referring to the recent election successes of far-right party Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Anke Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explains. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world. Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border: "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want." That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," thinks Lea Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
articles.summary: The Greek coastguard says it has rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals.

blocks.text: At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.
The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.
Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.
One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".
The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.
The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.
More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.
The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.
Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.

Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is embroiled in a spying scandal. Could the AI chipmaker survive without him?

image.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, on Oct. 21. As the CEO is investigated to determine whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, analysts worry what the future would look like for Nvidia if Huang had to step down. (Markus Schre

blocks.text: Business·New

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has helmed the company since starting it in 1993, guiding it from a graphics card maker to the AI behemoth it is today. But with an investigation now underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and no clear successor in sight, analysts say a change at the top — if it were deemed necessary — would be massive.
Analysts say change at the top would be a big shakeup, but company would go on
Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.

But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.

The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.

items: Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims

blocks.text: In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.
"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.

Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.
"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."
'The king of tech'

Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.

An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon, Meta, Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.
Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.

items: Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair
Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky

blocks.text: From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.
"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.

Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang
Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.

Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.
The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.
Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.
No clear successor
With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.
"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.
If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.
But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.
The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That
"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.
While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.
O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.
Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang, O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.

Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.

"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
