articles.title: Israel’s president picks Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form government
articles.summary:
Knesset has been deadlocked since election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority

Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s…

blocks.text: Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to ⁠try to ​form a new government, following a deadlocked election that left neither man ⁠with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu, ​Israel’s ‌longest-serving leader, ‌is fighting to hold on to office ‌after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc ‌in parliament.
An anti-Netanyahu grouping led by Eisenkot, an ​ex-military chief, has refused to join forces with Arab parties who could hand it a ⁠majority.
But Arab leaders, angered ​by ​policies of Netanyahu ​and his far-right allies, ​still ‌nominated Eisenkot during ​marathon ​talks with Herzog.

articles.title: New Zealand facing weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
articles.summary:
National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time

New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next…

blocks.text: New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.

On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by prime minister Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside his two traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.

But with some seats won by very slim margins, and a large tranche of special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.

Special votes, which include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate, are yet to be counted. In 2023, 600,000 votes were issued, or 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.

With nearly 100% of the votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just 3 seats behind.

Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight on Saturday, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could get under way.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.

Labour – led by Chris Hipkins – meanwhile, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori won five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party – Opportunity – the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.

blocks.caption: Labour party leader Chris Hipkins speaks to a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt on Saturday. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters

blocks.text: Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.

“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final vote land in its favour.

The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high ⁠inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helping propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.

Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need them to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, their predicted role could come to fruition.

Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from other larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters get to make two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
Te Pāti Māori, Act and New Zealand First urged voters to embrace strategic voting to try to maximise their share of MPs.
National has won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an additional five seats to make up the balance.

That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With those extra seats, there could be 130 seats in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.

The country will now face a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Caretaker government conventions will apply in the meantime, Luxon said.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

articles.title: New Zealand election coalition talks will likely take weeks – as it happened
articles.summary: • This blog is closed, you can read our report on the New Zealand election…

blocks.text: Closing summary
Thanks for following the blog tonight. The election has ended without a clear winner. Here are the top news lines from what will go down as one of New Zealand’s closest elections in many decades.

items: Christopher Luxon’s National party and its right-leaning coalition partners are on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a return to power.
The left-wing bloc, led by Labour’s Chris Hipkins, fell short of a majority.
Neither Luxon or Hipkins claimed victory or conceded defeat. Both acknowledged an expected wait before a governing coalition is negotiated.
A centrist newcomer, the Opportunity party, has entered parliament, polling above the 5% threshold. They could potentially be a kingmaker in a coalition.
Final results are expected on 27 November. Coalition talks will likely take weeks.
Hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted and could change the shape of parliament.
Saturday figures showed there could be a 130-seat parliament, with 66 seats needed for a majority.
Results suggested a coalition of National, Act and NZ First would hold 67 seats.
The 67 included 42 for National, 13 for Act and 12 for NZ First.
The left-bloc totalled 56 seats: Labour 35, Greens 16 and 5 for Te Pāti Māori.
Opportunity is projected to gain 7 seats.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3d agoClosing summary
3d agoRight-bloc just ahead with 97% of vote counted
3d agoGovernment 'caretaker conventions' will apply
3d agoLuxon calls the vote 'an MMP special'
3d agoNational 0.3% ahead of Labour with 85% of vote counted
3d agoNational just in front with 75% of votes counted

3d agoOverhang - what is it and how could it happen?
3d agoNational leading as 17% of vote counted
3d agoChris v Chris: know the difference
3d agoLet the count begin

blocks.text: Over the coming days and weeks we will get a sense of the magnitude of Qiulae Wong and the Opportunity party’s success tonight. Opportunity are currently projected to claim seven seats in parliament.

Wong has said that if she held the tiebreaker power, she was open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government and would deal first with whichever major party won the most votes.

blocks.caption: The Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong reacts as she arrives at a party gathering in Auckland. Photograph: Jonathan Killick/STUFF/AP

blocks.text: The right-wing bloc might not need her, and Luxon has ruled out governing with Opportunity. Analysts say, however, that both major party leaders would likely answer the phone if Wong held the only path to power.
You can read more about the rise of Opportunity here, in this piece from Michelle Duff.
A couple of pics of Christopher Luxon as he arrived to speak to supporters tonight.

blocks.caption: Photograph: Michael Bradley/AFP/Getty Images
Photograph: David Rowland/Reuters

blocks.text: On the current count, the Greens are celebrating a best-ever result of what looks to be 16 seats in parliament.
With 0.56% support, Te Pāti Māori will be stoked with its result tonight, writes Jamie Tahana.
It seems odd, but the Māori party has spent the election deliberately asking people not to give them their party vote. Instead, they asked for electorate votes only.
Just a reminder, seven of the seats in New Zealand’s parliament are reserved for representatives of Māori voters – you can read more about them here.

The party’s co-leaders, Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, have comfortably won their respective seats of Waiariki and Te Tai Hauauru; Oriini Kaipara swept the Auckland seat of Tamaki Makaurau; Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who hit international stardom for her haka in parliament, has cruised across the line in Hauraki-Waikato; while Aperahama Edwards holds a narrow lead over the Greens’ Hūhana Lydon in the far North seat of Te Tai Tokerau.
That’s five seats. But with a party vote so low, they will be five overhang seats.

Still, after a term that has seen plenty of in-fighting in Te Pāti Māori, there are signs of frustration in the Māori electorate, with Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer seeing significantly reduced majorities.

blocks.caption: Members of Te Pāti Māori in parliament, in 2025.  Photograph: Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP

blocks.text: The Greens have fallen short of gaining their first ever Māori electorate, but across the seats party vote has risen to about 40%, making the party a significant force in Māori politics.

Labour, having been punished by the Māori electorate in 2023, has improved, particularly in terms of party vote, and has claimed a new MP in Mananui Ramsden, who won the country’s largest electorate, Te Tai Tonga.
So, hundreds of thousands of special votes are going to potentially change where things stand right now.
In his speech tonight, Luxon said 300,000 special votes were yet to be counted. Those votes, which will be counted and known by 27 November, typically sway left.
In the 2023 election there 600,000 special votes, and National dropped from 50 seats in the preliminary count to 48 seats.
Right-bloc just ahead with 97% of vote counted

In a 130-seat parliament, in which 66 seats are needed to govern, this is where things stand with 97% of the vote counted. However, special votes are still to be counted and the lay of the land will not be clear until 27 November.
National 42, Act 13, NZ First 12 = 67
Labour 35, Greens 16, Te Pāti Māori 5 = 56
Opportunity 7
Numbers… with 97% of the vote counted:
National 29.3%, Labour 29.2%, Greens 13.3%, Act 11%, NZ First 9.8%, Opportunity 6%, Te Pāti Māori 0.6%.
Jamie Tahana has this hot-take on the Luxon speech:

It was a tough line to tread for a speech: National is the biggest party on current results – 29.30% – but Luxon has also led the party to one of its most unpopular points, only 0.1% ahead of Labour. Luxon has also lost some of his most senior and experienced MPs, which he conceded required “some tough phone calls”.
Government 'caretaker conventions' will apply
Luxon said that because of the closeness of the result, and with special votes still to be counted, caretaker conventions will apply.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”
Caretaker convention basically means that while a new government is being formed, the incumbent government is in “caretaker” mode, which means it will carry on the normal business of governing.
Jamie Tahana notes that for Luxon to continue as prime minister, he will have to cobble together a three- or four-party coalition, from a weakened position compared to 2023.
In his speech, Luxon said: “Negotiations and compromises are going to be required … A number of races are still too close to call.”
Jamie Tahana has some more from the Luxon speech:
Luxon called the election “too close to call”, and said “meaningful negotiations” for a new coalition government will start after the final results are known on 27 November.
“It looks like an MMP special,” he said. “It’s heartening to see that so far National is once again the largest party in parliament and we have a path to forming the next government.”
Luxon concedes result unlikely tonight, saying that meaningful negotiations will begin after final results on 27 November.

blocks.caption: Eva Corlett

blocks.text: Eva Corlett

Luxon arrived to a crowd of about 700 raucous supporters chanting “three more years”. He was flanked by his wife Amanda and two children, waved and grinned as he descended a stairwell flanked in blue light.
A heavy music track - which could not be immediately identified through Shazam - thrummed as he walked down a long aisle, hugging supporters.
When he took the podium, Luxon conceded the election was “too close to call” but the crowd cheered as he announced National had secured the highest party count.
He went on to acknowledge Labour leader Chris Hipkins, and admonished supporters who booed Quilae Wong and Opportunity, saying it was “not the kiwi way”.

Luxon is also paying tribute to those high-ranking National MPs who find themselves out of a job tonight: Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee. “I want to thank you … for your years of service to our party”.
Luxon calls the vote 'an MMP special'
Luxon has called tonight’s result “an MMP special” and says “on the numbers so far, National is once again the largest party in parliament”.
It will be interesting to see what Luxon has to say. How will he frame the vote count and National’s performance?
Christopher Luxon is high-fiving and hugging supporters. He’ll be speaking soon.
